Whether or not US president fits the definition of a Russian asset, his actions align closely with the Kremlin’s interests Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Luke Harding Wed 2 Sep 2026 10.30 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 10.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google C ould Donald Trump be a Russian asset? The headline on a review in the Guardian of my new book Betrayal has provoked heated international debate. Written by the historian Lawrence Freedman, the piece generated thousands of comments from across Europe and beyond on social media. Many people responded with a single word: “Duh!” Trump’s relationship with Vladimir Putin is the biggest mystery in international politics. In 2017 I wrote a book called Collusion , which set out Moscow’s operation to support and cultivate Trump, going back decades. The US president, of course, denies links with Russia. But in his second term, his behaviour towards Putin has been as weird and perplexing as during his first. For example, at the Alaska summit last year the US president applauded his Russian counterpart, meeting him at Anchorage airport and rolling out a red carpet. Trump seemed uncharacteristically nervous, as he waited for Putin to emerge from his plane. At their joint press conference after talks, he allowed the Russian president to speak first. It was a bizarre act of deference. Why? There are, I think, overlapping reasons for Trump’s submissive behaviour. I explore them in Betrayal, (which is published this week in Denmark by Politikens Forlag, with Italian, Finnish and Ukrainian language editions to follow.) View image in fullscreen Danish book cover of Luke Harding’s Betrayal Illustration: Politikens Forlag As I mentioned in a Q&A with Guardian readers , one factor is ideological: Trump’s Maga supporters see Russia as an “anti-woke” kindred state. Putin leans into this idea, positioning himself as a defender of conservative values, under threat from a decadent and godless Europe. High-profile Trump supporters have travelled to Moscow. Erstwhile Maga cheerleader and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson even absurdly praised the Russian capital’s well-stocked supermarkets. Another explanation – advanced by Fiona Hill, the former White House adviser – is strongman envy. Trump would like Putin’s freedom of action, when it comes to making money and crushing opponents. It is evident the US president prefers the company of autocrats. By contrast he frequently badmouths European democrats, among them the former British PM Keir Starmer (“no Churchill”) , and Giorgia Meloni (“I felt sorry for her”.) A third theory is kompromat , a KGB term to describe potential compromising material. We know from declassified records that the Czechoslovakia secret police began spying on Trump in the 1970s , when he married a woman from behind the iron curtain. He visited Moscow in 1987, on a trip organised by a Soviet state agency, and subsequently made many visits to Russia including in 2013 for the Miss Universe beauty pageant. What exactly happened on these excursions is unclear. But I know from my own experience in Moscow – I was the Guardian’s bureau chief from 2007 to 2011 – that Russia’s intelligence agencies are adept at surveillance operations . Shortly after I arrived, the FSB broke into the apartment I shared with my wife and our two children. They left clues, busting open the window in my son’s bedroom, with a perilous drop to the courtyard below. The British embassy advised us our home was bugged. Possibly, Putin’s ghost-like spies had installed video cameras too, we were told. Over the next four years we experienced on-off harassment from a shadowy and paranoid state. There were mysterious break-ins, veiled threats from foreign ministry officials, and a summons to visit Lefortovo, the FSB’s infamous pre-detention centre and gloomy prison. Undoubtedly, the KGB and FSB will have spied on Trump too, as well as on other high-profile foreign guests. A 2020 report by the US Senate intelligence committee alleged that the FSB has secret cameras inside the Ritz-Carlton hotel , where Trump stayed during his 2013 trip. There will be tapes. They may be innocuous. But Putin knows what they show, and Trump knows that Putin knows. Consequences remain the same skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Russia continues to bombard Kyiv as the US refuses to send Patriot interceptors to Ukraine. Photograph: Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP/Getty Images Does this make Trump an asset? My conclusion is that the terminology doesn’t much matter. As the chess champion Garry Kasparov notes, if Trump were an asset, or an agent of influence, what exactly would he do differently? Since 2025 he has stopped direct US military aid to Kyiv, humiliated Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office , and repeated Kremlin lies and disinformation. The US president’s Russia-friendly actions have consequences. I have been visiting Kyiv for nearly two decades, and have spent much of the past five years reporting from Ukraine and the frontline. I was in the capital in February 2022 when Putin tried to seize it. Since then, the conflict has evolved. It is no longer fought with armoured vehicles and tanks, and has become instead a hi-tech aerial battle. Most nights, Russia bombards Kyiv with kamikaze drones and ballistic missiles. Ukraine, meanwhile, carries out its own long-range strikes . It has the world’s most innovative drone and counter-drone industry. But Kyiv badly lacks US-made Patriot interceptors – the only system capable of shooting down fast-moving ballistic missiles. Trump refuses to send Patriots or allow Kyiv to develop its own version under licence. And so civilians die – families, elderly couples, teenagers – entombed under the ruins of pulverised apartment blocks. At night you hear explosions, a moped-like growl from enemy drones, and booms from Ukrainian air defence. Asset or not, Trump is doing little to make this horror stop. Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest, is published in the UK by Guardian Faber. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . https://www.politico.eu/article/a-common.text: Europe’s existential challenges keep piling up . From rising energy bills and defense spending to a dizzying race for AI leadership, the €1.2 trillion in annual investment the continent needs to stay competitive looks increasingly like an underestimate. Addressing these challenges cannot come at the expense of the resources needed to strengthen integration, solidarity and a robust welfare state — core elements of the European project and our safest bet for securing the EU’s place on the world stage. As Europe rushes to unify its capital markets and mobilize trillions of euros in idle household savings, it should also pursue a long-term financial framework that breaks with its reactive past. Instead, we are moving in the opposite direction. Advertisement Advertisement Louder calls to slash the EU’s 2028–2034 financial framework will prevent Europe from acting on its own terms in a hostile world. The European Commission’s original proposal of almost €2 trillion varies little from the current spending plan once repayments of the post-pandemic recovery grants are excluded. That amounts to roughly 1.15% of the EU’s gross national income (GNI). To get the debate back on track, Spain has proposed freeing up to €11 billion a year in resources that make both financial and political sense. Instead of repaying the debt associated with the grant component of NextGenerationEUfaster than required, the EU should link its service to its long-term economic capacity. An annual payment of about 0.06% of EU GDP would retire the debt by 2058, the deadline agreed by member states. Under the current plan, repayments would amount to between 0.09% and 0.11% a year over the next seven years. Reprofiling the debt payment would free up nearly €70 billion over that period, whichis equivalent to about one-fifth of the proposed European Competitiveness Fund thatwould channel investment into strategic sectors. It also amounts to roughly one-third of the aid the EU has sent to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022. This approach would not only release extra resources but keep the stock of EU debt broadly stable in the medium term while sending a strong signal to investors who are demanding more euro-denominated assets. The proposal can also be seen as part of a more ambitious strategy to develop a European safe asset that drags down the liquidity premium that investors are asking for. Separately, Spain has proposed allowing the Commission to issue a portion of member countries’ debt on their behalf, helping to create a deeper common market for European debt. This could generate €25 billion in annual interest savings. Advertisement Advertisement With Spain for the first time set to become a net contributor to the next long-term budget, we are more than willing to pay our fair share to help make the EU a global powerhouse that creates opportunities for its citizens. The next framework should have a ceiling equivalent to 2% of EU GNI — enough to support both the economy and society. That figure would still fall well short of the investment gap identified by Mario Draghi and Enrico Letta. But it would at least begin to address the concerns of investors and citizens. The size of the next budget will send an important message to voters ahead of elections next year that will take more than half of the EU population to the polls. Populist far-right parties are making political gains by offering simple answers to complicated problems — and blaming the EU in the process. Europeans need economic security. They need reassurance that their energy bills will not soar again and that their factories will stay open. In the most challenging decade since the Cold War, this is not the time for Europe to make itself smaller. Doing so would play into the hands of populists intent on dismantling the European project. Through initiatives such as NextGenerationEU, Europe came together to provide much-needed economic security. It took a crisis to get us there. The task now is to build on that progress and get back on track before the next one. Advertisement Advertisement

Gaza: Devastation inside Nasser Hospital after deadly Israeli strike Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 12 November 2026 - 17:10 GMT+1 An Israeli airstrike hit Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, early on Thursday 12 November, killing six people, including a doctor, and injuring at least 27 others, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). … More The strike devastated the hospital's surgical department , with damage also reported to operating theatres, recovery facilities and the intensive care unit. Footage shows extensive destruction inside the hospital, with shattered ceilings, twisted metal and rubble scattered across medical equipment and beds. Rescue workers searched through the debris, while grieving relatives gathered outside to pray over the bodies of those killed. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Gaza's Health Ministry identified one of the victims as general surgeon Rizk Abu Shaira . The Israeli military acknowledged carrying out the strike , saying it had targeted a senior Hamas commander and other militants allegedly operating from the hospital, but provided no evidence to substantiate its claims . The attack struck one of the few remaining functioning hospitals in Gaza , where years of war have devastated healthcare services and left medical facilities struggling to meet overwhelming needs. According to the WHO, 1,056 attacks on healthcare facilities and personnel have been documented in Gaza since October 2023, resulting in 1,010 deaths and 1,725 injuries . The organisation warned that approaching winter conditions, including heavy rain, flooding and cold temperatures, could further worsen the humanitarian crisis, particularly as water and sanitation systems remain severely damaged. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using hospitals for military purposes , allegations the group denies. Under international humanitarian law, hospitals and medical personnel are protected , although facilities can lose specific protections if used to commit acts harmful to the enemy, subject to strict conditions. The WHO reiterated its call for unhindered humanitarian access and the protection of medical facilities .
